# Demand prediction {#sec-demand-prediction}
To answer the question whether demand can be predicted from calendar, weather and location information alone and if a deep learning approach is justified if increasing the complexity. To predict the demand in a spatial unit at a specific time two models, Neural Network and Support Vector Machines, are trained and compared based on different spatial and temporal units.
To have a baseline of what is expected we use a simple historical average per spatial unit and time window. The average is computed on the training set and applied to the test set. For the baseline, the normalized MAE of 0.31 shows that on average the prediction is off by 31% of the actual demand. The two models are assessed and compared using the normalized MAE and R² on the test set. The normalized MAE is the mean absolute error divided by the mean demand, which allows for a fair comparison across different spatial and temporal resolutions. R² is the coefficient of determination, which measures how well the model explains the variance in the data. The higher the R², the better the model fits the data. The results of the two models are presented in the following sections.

## Support Vector Machines (SVM)
As we predict a continuous demand value, we use Support Vector Regression (SVR). SVR comes with three different kernel functions which were all tested: linear, polynomial and radial basis function (RBF). The SVR is trained on a subset of the data, as it scales roughly quadratically with the number of samples. In the optimization steps 20,000 rows of the training set are used. The final model is trained on a 50,000-row subsample of the training set and evaluated on the test set.
Four approaches for SVR were tested, resulting in 24 configurations. The following design dimensions are varied: (i) the spatial resolution (448 census tracts or 77 community areas), (ii) the temporal resolution(1h, 4h or 1d), (iii) the target transformation (none or log1p), and (iv) target encoding ^[Target encoding adds one column containing the mean trip count per spatial unit, computed on the training set, so the model learns whether a location is generally busy or quiet.] (with or without). This is assessed in 4 phases, each varying one factor while keeping the others fixed to isolate the effect of every design decision while still providing the best SVR model. The full feature set can be found in @tbl-svr-features in Appendix -@sec-app-svr-features.  A hyperparameter grid search ensures that for each configuration the best kernel type and hyperparameters are selected. Before evaluating, we verified that the chronological test set is representative of the training data; the target distributions of both splits are compared in @fig-svr-train-test-dist.

@tbl-svr-phases shows the various phases and the corresponding configurations. Comparing the two spatial layers (i) shows that community areas outperform census tracts (R² 0.84 against 0.63, rMAE 0.44 against 1.17). In a second step, target encoding^[Dummy encoding was rejected because it would add up to 448 sparse columns, which is computationally expensive given the quadratic scaling of kernel SVR.] (iv) was tested. While it only affectes the rMAE for community areas (0.68 instead of 0.44), it improves census tracts R² from 0.22 to 0.66. log1p is tested in phase 3 (iii) and behaves similarly at 1h, where R² stays the same and only the error improves, but at 4h the transform lifts R² from 0.88 to 0.89 and reduces rMAE from 0.39 to 0.32. Lastly, the temporal resolution (ii) is varied. Wider time windows improve every metric (R² 0.83 to 0.88 to 0.93) because aggregation averages out short-term noise. Across the grid, the polynomial kernel performs best on the untransformed target, while the RBF kernel wins whenever log1p is applied. A visual comparison of all three kernel families can be found in @fig-svr-kernel-comparison and the full results across all 24 configurations are shown in @tbl-svr-full-grid.

The best raw performance is community areas at daily resolution without target encoding and the RBF kernel (R² 0.93, rMAE 0.23). Since a daily total per neighborhood is too coarse for actual fleet coordination, we select community areas at 4h with target encoding, log1p and an RBF kernel (R² 0.89, rMAE 0.32) as the final SVR benchmark against the neural network. The full discussion of which resolution the client should deploy follows in the final recommendation.

This leaves the model with three notable shortfalls. The scaling cap described above means the SVR never sees more than a fraction of the available data. The log1p transform, needed to handle the skewed target, compresses high values and therefore tends to under-predict extreme peaks, which are exactly the baskets that matter most on event days. And at fine spatial resolution the model depends entirely on manual feature engineering. Without target encoding, census tract performance collapses. For a follow-up project, the clearest improvement levers target the scaling cap directly. Kernel approximations such as Nyström would reduce the quadratic cost to a linear one and let the SVR train on the full dataset, while gradient-boosted trees such as LightGBM handle large sample sizes and non-linear interactions natively and would replace the kernel machinery altogether. The error distribution per community area for the recommended configuration can be found in @fig-svr-error-boxplot.
